nameStory: The rough barnacle gets its name from the distinctly coarse, bumpy texture of its shell plates, which feel noticeably rougher to the touch than its smoother barnacle cousins. The scientific name 'Balanus' comes from the Latin word for acorn, referring to the acorn-like shape that gives all acorn barnacles their common name.
description: Rough barnacles are small marine crustaceans that cement themselves permanently to rocks, docks, and other hard surfaces in cold ocean waters. They build cone-shaped, white to grayish shells made of overlapping plates that can grow up to about an inch across. Despite looking like mollusks, they're actually more closely related to crabs and lobsters, extending feathery legs through the top opening to filter food from the water.

idTips.label: Shell texture
idTips.description: The shell plates feel distinctly rough and bumpy when you run your finger across them, like coarse sandpaper, much rougher than other common barnacles

idTips.label: Shell shape
idTips.description: Forms a broad, cone-shaped structure with 6 thick wall plates that fit together like puzzle pieces, creating a sturdy acorn-like appearance

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Generally grows larger than most other barnacles in New England waters, often reaching nearly an inch in diameter at the base

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Shell plates range from dirty white to light gray, sometimes with darker streaks or staining from algae growth

idTips.label: Attachment
idTips.description: Firmly cemented to hard surfaces with such strength that removing one often breaks the shell rather than the bond

habitat: Look for rough barnacles attached to rocky shores, pier pilings, and breakwaters in the colder waters of northern New England, especially along the Maine coast. They prefer areas with good water circulation and are typically found in the lower intertidal zone where they're submerged most of the time.

seasonality.spring: Adults become more active as water temperatures rise, extending their feeding appendages more frequently during high tide.
seasonality.summer: Peak feeding and growth period when the feathery legs are most visible during high tide as they filter plankton from the water.
seasonality.fall: Reproductive season when larvae are released into the water column to settle on new surfaces.
seasonality.winter: Barnacles remain tightly closed during harsh weather and low temperatures, appearing inactive but surviving well in cold water.

funFact: Rough barnacles start life as free-swimming larvae that must find the perfect spot to settle within just a few days, then literally glue their heads to that surface and spend the rest of their lives standing on their heads, kicking food into their mouths with their legs!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the more common wrinkled barnacle, but rough barnacles feel much coarser when touched and grow noticeably larger. Memory trick: 'rough and robust' - they're both rougher textured and bigger than their relatives.
contextualKnowledge: Many people don't realize that barnacles are crustaceans (like crabs and shrimp) rather than mollusks, which explains why they have jointed, feathery legs instead of the soft bodies you'd expect from something living in a shell.
compareHints: Rough barnacles are larger and much more coarsely textured than wrinkled barnacles, which have smoother shells with fine ridges. Triangle barnacles have a more distinctly triangular profile when viewed from the side, while rough barnacles maintain a more evenly rounded cone shape.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wrinkled barnacles are much smaller and more delicately built than their cousin the rough barnacle, with distinctly ridged shells that feel gritty to touch.
Unlike its relatives the wrinkled barnacle and rough barnacle, which are more circular or oval-shaped, the triangle barnacle has that distinctive three-sided form.
